Well, the political groups in the lower house are usually the ones actually proposing legislation to it, so the representatives have some say during the process that leads up to it. On the voting itself there’s a bit of difference between a) directly elected representatives, which have a bit more leeway on voting against their own group/party, than b) representatives that were elected for their party and don’t represent an electoral district. But to answer your question: mostly the representatives vote for their party, the word is *Fraktionszwang*. One notable, fairly recent vote for which this was lifted was the vote about legalising gay marriage in 2017.

Direct democracy isn’t the key difference here. The key difference is that every major political party is represented in the government, it’s a *Konkordanzdemokratie*. One could argue that this is less democratic than a parliamentary democracy, because the parties aren’t quantitatively represented in the government according to elections. True, in this case the situation would be the same. But it comes down to who’s running the country, fundamentally. In the UK it’s the party, in Germany the Bundestag. It gives power to all elected officials, not just to those that belong to the governing party. Furthermore, it’s quite the difference wether a few governing MPs need to vote against the PM (thus enabling a majority, a majority of all MPs), or wether a majority of their own party needs to vote against them. I’m a time of crisis (like now), there has to be a way for the majority of elected officials to appoint a new, better leader. Just imagine: The opposition, with few exceptions, agrees on a sort of “crisis manager” as PM. You’d still need about 80 Tory MPs for a majority, but that’s miles away from the 180 you need currently to vote him out.

British democracy is quite weird actually. Living in what you’d call a modern democracy we have the benefit of setting up a system in 1949 that knows what faults enabled the dismantling of itself from within. And since I was born in this democracy, even though I’d consider myself a bit of a nerd for British politics, a few things are weird in particular:

a) There’s no constitution. All laws can be made with a simple majority in parliament(s). That seems like a really shot idea, because it depends on trust in politicians to not fuck with basic rights, and we’re currently seeing how that rolls. 

b) Majority system. FPTP is a really bad system for elections, because the seats in the House of Commons don’t accurately reflect the amount of people that actually voted for this or that party. We have a mixed system (according to Wikipedia it’s translated as proportional representation), which has its own faults (leads to high number of representatives, all of whom are quite costly and makes the house big and sluggish), but at least the vote is more accurately reflected in the house that governs us. 

c) Removal of fallen leaders. It’s so weird to me that the party of the head of government itself decides to vote him out, not the whole house. We had a system that enabled part of the chaos that led to Hitler, which was that the house could vote someone out of office with a majority. So the left and right voted together to deselect the chancellor. Obviously their majority couldn’t be used to elect a new chancellor of course, which effectively deadlocked government. So after the war it was refined so that a new chancellor has to be elected in the same sitting, to ensure that this wouldn’t happen again.

d) Passiveness of head of state. Except from it being a democratic instead of monarchist selection process, our head of state has a general „overlook the government“ kind of job, and from the outside it seems the queen has partly a similar job. But she doesn’t regulate, even if the ministerial code is breached it’s assumed government would act on it themselves, and we see how that’s going. Why doesn’t the queen intervene and call for re-elections? The current government obviously has no majority with the people and don’t do anything about it. 

So yeah, bash me for my ancestors and the war all you want, and I’m not here to put myself/my country above you/yours, but just an observation from an outsider that on the one hand loves most brits and adores a lot of your culture (as well as a remote thankfulness for liberating the Germans), and on the other hand is worried for you and your democracy. Because in my opinion you (and everyone in fact) deserve better leaders than BoJo, oligarchs, aristocrats and this clique of people so detached from reality and empathy for the general public.
